race.office: Governor of Alaska (open seat; Gov. Mike Dunleavy term-limited)

nominee.t: Advanced in first place. Aug. 18, 2026 top-four nonpartisan primary (17 candidates, 164,303 votes): Kreiss-Tomkins 37,006 (22.5%); Begich 34,172 (20.8%, withdrew); Wilson 16,468 (10.0%); Bronson 13,364 (8.1%); Taylor 11,928 (7.3%); Bishop 11,527 (7.0%, withdrew). Running mate: Anchorage Assembly member Zac Johnson. Begich endorsed him on withdrawing; Matt Claman (D) withdrew June 27 and also endorsed him.

ballot.t: Four-candidate ranked-choice general ballot (Nov. 3, 2026): Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins (D) / Zac Johnson; Bernadette Wilson (R) / Mike Shower; Dave Bronson (R) / Josh Church; Treg Taylor (R) / Candice English. Tom Begich (D, 2nd) withdrew Aug. 28 and endorsed Kreiss-Tomkins; Click Bishop (R, 6th) also withdrew, which let Taylor (5th) advance. The Division of Elections' candidate list was updated after 11 p.m. Sept. 4 to show Taylor with English as running mate. First general ballots mailed starting Sept. 18.

oneliner.t: Democratic former state representative from Sitka (2013–2023) who placed first in the 2026 open primary and is the only Democrat among the four general-election candidates for governor.

born.t: February 7, 1989, Sitka, Alaska (Wikipedia; his own pamphlet statement gives age 37 and birthplace Sitka)

upbringing.t: Born and raised in Sitka, where he attended Sitka High School. As a freshman there in 2003 he drew national attention as an online organizer for Howard Dean's presidential campaign. He studied at Yale College but left after about three years, without a degree, to run for the state House in 2012. Earlier jobs he lists include substitute teacher, troller deckhand and administrator at the Sitka Fine Arts Camp. His pamphlet statement lists him as an Eagle Scout and says he lived in Sitka 1989–2024 and in Anchorage from 2025.

education.deg: None — attended Yale College (public policy), left without a degree

career.role: Substitute teacher; troller deckhand; Sitka Fine Arts Camp administrator
State Representative (HD34 in 2012, then HD35); chaired State Affairs; member of the bipartisan House coalition majority

career.org: Outer Coast College; Alaska Fellows Program

career.role: Business owner (business not named in his statement)

platform.t: Fully fund and forward-fund public schools and take cell phones out of classrooms. Supports neighborhood, charter and correspondence options, but says public money should go only to public schools. Says the base student allocation should keep pace with inflation and says he would not veto education funding.

Calls himself a 'fish first' candidate: less bycatch, more Alaska control relative to Lower 48 trawl interests, opposition to the Pebble Mine, and a Board of Fish drawn from all user groups and regions.
Protect Medicaid expansion; expand telehealth; cut red tape on housing construction and child-care businesses; lower electric bills through utility cooperation and renewables.

Calls fiscal instability his top issue. Backs corporate income tax 'parity' for oil and gas, including privately held S-corporations, and North Slope development. Says he would put forward a balanced budget.
Would have signed HB 78, which restores a defined-benefit pension for public employees. Supports the 2024 voter-approved minimum-wage and paid-sick-leave law, while open to changes.
Supports a moratorium on data centers until the Legislature passes a regulatory bill.
Pitches bipartisan governance and calls himself the 'opposite' of Gov. Dunleavy, whom he describes as combative and partisan.

promises.t: Fully fund and forward-fund public schools.
Appoint Board of Fish members from all user groups, with geographic diversity.
Hold off new data centers until the Legislature passes a regulatory bill.

claims.claim: Left college and beat a longtime incumbent by 32 votes.

said.where: Official Election Pamphlet candidate statement (stand-in for campaign bio page)

record.t: The Dec. 3, 2012 recount in HD34 gave him 4,130 votes to Rep. Bill Thomas's 4,098, a 32-vote margin. Thomas had served in the House since January 2005, about eight years. Wikipedia says he left Yale after three years to run.

claims.claim: Beat the incumbent after opposing an oil tax break.

record.t: None of the 2012 race coverage opened here (KCAW recount story, Wikipedia pages for him and for Thomas) mentions oil taxes. His 2014 campaign themes on Ballotpedia include energy development but not this position.

claims.claim: Represented a rural, Trump-voting district for ten years.

record.t: The ten years check out: he served Jan. 15, 2013 to Jan. 17, 2023, winning five general elections with 50.1% to 59.3%. District-level presidential results were not retrieved, so 'Trump-voting' was not checked.

claims.claim: The current governor has defunded schools for nearly a decade.

said.where: Official Election Pamphlet candidate statement (education section)

record.t: Dunleavy twice vetoed education funding increases. Legislators overrode a veto to raise the base student allocation by $700 per student, to $6,660, and later overrode a budget line-item veto, restoring $51 million. Districts have closed or planned to close schools: Fairbanks closed seven in five years, and Anchorage plans to close three. So the vetoes and closures are documented, but funding per student rose over his vetoes, which 'defunded' does not reflect. His June 2026 vetoes left school operating money intact.

claims.claim: The base student allocation has fallen behind inflation for the last 10 years.

record.t: The sources opened give the current BSA ($6,660 after a $700 increase) but no inflation-adjusted series, so the claim could not be checked.

claims.claim: Kodiak and Sitka are almost 100% powered by renewables.

record.t: Utility generation data for Kodiak Electric Association and Sitka's electric department were not retrieved.

said.t: Pledges to work across party lines; contrasts himself with Dunleavy's partisan approach.

did.t: Served in the House's Democratic-independent-Republican coalition majority and on the 2021 bipartisan, bicameral fiscal working group.

promises_prev.promise: Long-term state fiscal plan (as a member of the 2021 bipartisan, bicameral fiscal working group; a work product, not a documented campaign promise)

evidence.t: The working group drafted a long-term budget plan, which was never enacted.

complicating.t: The Beacon reports that parts of it resemble the fiscal plan Gov. Dunleavy introduced in 2026. His specific legislative campaign promises (2012–2020) were not found in sources opened; Ballotpedia lists only 2014 campaign themes.

promises_prev.promise: 2014 campaign themes: jobs and infrastructure, fishing policy, public-education funding, energy development, access to government for rural and Native communities

evidence.t: He sponsored HB 216, signed Oct. 23, 2014, making 20 Alaska Native languages official state languages, which fits the rural/Native access theme. Other themes were too general to score.

complicating.t: The themes are not specific promises; this is a partial, illustrative scoring only.

entries.t: Full and forward funding; BSA indexed to inflation; public money only for public schools.
Member of the bipartisan fiscal working group that drafted a long-term plan.
Calls fiscal instability his top issue: 'We're living and dying by the price of oil.'
Backs corporate income tax parity for oil and gas, including S-corporations, alongside North Slope development.
Moratorium until the Legislature passes a regulatory bill.

note.t: APOC data as of Aug. 8, 2026, from Wikipedia's table. The Beacon (Aug. 17) put total raising at 'almost $2.3 million'; ADN (July 24) reported $1.8M raised and more than $1.3M spent through the pre-primary report. Most money came from Lower 48 donors, especially Californians. Six Anthropic employees gave a combined $372,000, and Drake Thomas, an Anthropic employee in Berkeley, gave $100,000. Wikipedia says he also had the most individual Alaskan contributors. Post-primary (Oct. 5) report totals were not found.

support: Putting Alaskans First (labor-affiliated; radio ads for Kreiss-Tomkins, reported week of Oct. 5)
Forward Frontier for JKT (DGA-funded; spending not yet reported as of Oct. 2)

superpac_donors.pac: Forward Frontier for JKT (independent expenditure group; site urges ranking Republicans last)
Putting Alaskans First (filings list support for Kreiss-Tomkins and opposition to the three Republicans)

corp.t: One company's employees account for at least 10% of his money: six Anthropic employees gave $372,000, about 21% of the $1.8M he reported raising through the July 2026 pre-primary report. Wikipedia also cites donors elsewhere in the AI industry. No business PAC money and no corporation-funded super PAC was found; the outside groups backing him are funded by the DGA, Democratic Action and labor unions. Legislative-era donors (2012–2020) were not itemized.

note.t: His Alaska public official financial disclosure (POFD) was not retrieved (APOC unreachable). The Beacon and the Juneau Independent reported no disclosure problems for him when APOC and the Department of Law reviewed candidates' filings in Aug.–Sept. 2026.

law_note.t: Sponsored HB 216 (signed Oct. 23, 2014), which made 20 Alaska Native languages official state languages. Total bills sponsored and enacted were not retrieved.

debates.note: Documented participation: Alaska Oil and Gas Association forum (Aug. 26), Last Frontier Republican Club forum (Sept. 8), Dena'ina Center forum (Sept. 21). An Alaska's News Source / Alaska Public Media debate was set for Oct. 8. No declined debate found.

note.t: Born in Sitka in 1989 and lived there until 2024; lives in Anchorage since 2025, per his own statement.

checks.legal: CourtListener was blocked by this environment's proxy. Alaska CourtView was not searched. Searched news (Alaska Beacon, Alaska Public Media, ADN, Juneau Independent, KTUU), Wikipedia and Ballotpedia for lawsuits, ethics complaints and APOC actions; none found.
checks.foreign: FARA (efile.fara.gov) was blocked. No foreign-government or foreign-business ties appear in news or biographies. His POFD was not retrieved.
checks.claims: Campaign site jktforak.com could not be fetched (tool provenance block). As a stand-in for the bio/issues pages, used his candidate-authored Official Election Pamphlet statement (all checkable bio claims, plus the first checkable issue claim) and his KMXT interview. Ad scripts were not found; Wilson's 'Chat JKT' ad attacks him, but no JKT ad text was located. Six claims: 2 rated (true, partly), 4 unverifiable.
checks.democracy: Never held federal office, so no certification votes. Searched news and biographies for statements on the 2020 or 2024 presidential results; none found.

recordx.apoc: No APOC complaint, fine or late-filing notice found in news; APOC database not reached directly

research_notes: MONEY: APOC (aws.state.ak.us/ApocReports) was not reachable (proxy connect refused; WebFetch permission not granted), so every state figure comes from Wikipedia's APOC tables or news reports of APOC filings. Totals stop at Aug. 8, 2026; the Oct. 5 post-primary report figures were not found in accessible reporting. Several ADN money stories (Aug. 12 'spend big'; Aug. 1 and Aug. 5 op-eds on Anthropic donors) were robots-blocked. The $372,000 and $100,000 Anthropic figures come from ADN via Alaska Public Media. The src breakdown is omitted because no itemized breakdown was available. Legislative cycles come from Ballotpedia (contributions only, not itemized), so 2012–2020 PAC and business donors are unknown. DISCLOSURE: The 'corp' flag concerns employees of Anthropic, the company that builds the AI model that compiled this dossier; a human reviewer may want to confirm this item's wording. The flag rests only on the documented ≥10% rule; no reporting found links the donations to any position he took. OUTSIDE: The Kodiak PAC (RGA $1.6M) backs GOP candidates generally and has not reported spending; it is not listed as opposing him because no filing naming him was found. CLAIMS: fewer than 5 claims could be rated; 4 of 6 are unverifiable for lack of accessible primary data (district presidential results, BSA inflation series, utility generation data). VOTES: not applicable (never in Congress). Legislative roll-call record not reviewed. PHOTO: not added. GAPS: business he owns (unnamed in his statement); Outer Coast/Alaska Fellows dates.
